title: Comparative efficacy of different exercise modalities on renal function and glycemic control in patients with non-dialysis diabetic kidney disease: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
label: approved
note: Exercise for kidney function and blood sugar in diabetic kidney disease.
abstract:
Objective

To evaluate the comparative efficacy and safety of structured exercise modalities on renal function and glycemic control in non-dialysis diabetic kidney disease (DKD).

Design

Systematic review and network meta-analysis.

Data sources

Six databases (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang) were searched from inception to July 15, 2026.

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating structured exercise (aerobic, resistance, combined, or mind-body) versus usual care or an active comparator in adults with non-dialysis DKD (duration ≥4 weeks).

Outcome measures

Renal endpoints were estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and urinary albumin excretion (UAE); glycemic endpoints were glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) and fasting blood glucose (FBG).

Results

Twenty RCTs (1,746 patients) were included. Compared with usual care, resistance training (RT) was the sole modality significantly increasing eGFR (mean difference [MD] 11.36 mL/min/1.73 m², 95% CI 4.47 to 18.25; low certainty) and outperforming aerobic training (MD 8.61, 2.22 to 15.00). Mind-body exercise (MBE) was the only intervention significantly reducing UAE (standardized mean difference -1.41, -2.67 to -0.16; low certainty). For glycemic regulation, RT (MD -1.65%), aerobic training (MD -1.07%), and combined training (CT; MD -0.70%) significantly lowered HbA1c (all low certainty). Significant FBG reductions occurred only with RT (MD -1.78 mmol/L; low certainty) and CT (MD -1.71 mmol/L; moderate certainty). In sensitivity analyses, RT's eGFR benefit lost significance after excluding high-risk trials (MD 8.24, -1.17 to 17.64), and CT's HbA1c reduction was attenuated in pure-exercise models (MD -0.60%, -1.39 to 0.19). Subgroup analyses showed CT uniquely sustained FBG reductions across short-term (≤12 weeks: MD -1.50) and longer-term (>12 weeks: MD -2.39) regimens. Structured safety was monitored in only five trials (25.0%): three reported mild, transient events without serious harm, while two explicitly declared zero adverse events. Thus, current evidence is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions regarding comparative safety.

Conclusions

Structured exercise confers distinct adaptations in non-dialysis DKD. Combined training provides a reliable foundation for sustained glycemic management, while mind-body exercise represents a viable strategy for albuminuria. Resistance training's apparent renal benefit warrants caution due to fragility against bias. Prescriptions should be individualized rather than seeking a single optimal modality. Given the sparse monitoring of adverse events, comparative clinical safety cannot be definitively established and mandates routine surveillance.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD420261489091.

title: Physical exercise: a multi-target strategy for the prevention and treatment of Alzheimer's disease.
label: approved
note: Exercise and Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a devastating age-related neurodegenerative disease characterized by irreversible cognitive dysfunction and neuronal loss. The complex pathogenesis of AD involves core proteinopathies of amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau, chronic neuroinflammation, and extensive cerebral metabolic disorders, which collectively drive progressive neuronal damage and disease deterioration. Currently, effective disease-modifying drugs for AD are still lacking, and physical exercise has been recognized as a safe and effective non-pharmacological intervention to prevent and alleviate AD pathological progression. Specifically, exercise inhibits abnormal Aβ deposition and tau hyperphosphorylation, suppresses microglial overactivation and sustained neuroinflammatory responses, and remodels cerebral metabolic homeostasis by improving glucose utilization, balancing lactate metabolism, restoring mitochondrial function, and correcting dysregulated lipid metabolism. Additionally, exercise-mediated upregulation of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) enhances neuronal survival and synaptic plasticity to block AD pathological progression. This review innovatively combines core AD pathological markers and multi-dimensional metabolic mechanisms, providing a theoretical reference for further exploring the molecular mechanism of exercise intervention in AD.

title: Creatine and essential amino acids with exercise in obesity: an immunometabolic perspective on the muscle-adipose-brain axis.
label: approved
note: Creatine, amino acids and exercise in obesity.
abstract: Obesity is associated with anabolic resistance, skeletal muscle dysfunction, adipose tissue dysregulation, chronic low-grade inflammation, and altered brain metabolism. Exercise is a primary strategy for counteracting these disturbances, while nutritional interventions may complement exercise-induced adaptations. Creatine and essential amino acids (EAAs) have established roles in muscle bioenergetics and protein synthesis, respectively, but their combined use with exercise and potential effects on the interconnected muscle-adipose-brain axis in obesity remain incompletely characterized. This review examines mechanistic and clinical evidence for creatine and EAA supplementation alongside exercise, with emphasis on muscle anabolism, body composition, adipose remodeling, immunometabolism, and muscle-adipose-brain communication. Exercise provides the principal physiological stimulus for muscle adaptation, whereas EAAs, particularly leucine, stimulate muscle protein synthesis through amino acid-sensing and mTORC1-related pathways. Creatine increases phosphocreatine availability and may enhance training capacity, strength, and lean mass when combined with resistance exercise. Available evidence suggests potentially complementary, rather than established synergistic, effects of creatine and EAAs with exercise on muscle preservation, functional capacity, and body composition. Beyond muscle, exercise-derived myokines, exerkines, adipokines, and metabolites provide plausible mechanisms linking peripheral adaptations to adipose tissue and the brain. Creatine may support cellular and cerebral bioenergetics, whereas EAAs influence amino acid availability and protein turnover. However, direct evidence that these interventions modify obesity-associated neuroinflammation, depression, or cognitive dysfunction remains limited. Overall, current evidence supports exercise as the central intervention, with creatine and EAAs representing potentially complementary nutritional strategies. Evidence for integrated effects on adipose-brain communication, immunometabolism, and neurobehavioral outcomes remains preliminary and is derived substantially from indirect or preclinical findings. Future randomized trials should directly compare individual and combined interventions, establish optimal dosing and timing, and integrate mechanistic biomarkers with clinically relevant metabolic and neurobehavioral outcomes.

title: Resistance Training and Respiratory and Immune-Related Outcomes in Older Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
label: approved
note: Resistance training, lung and immune outcomes in older adults.
abstract: Age-related declines in pulmonary function and immune regulation increase morbidity and mortality in older adults. Physical activity mitigates these effects, but the isolated impact of resistance training (RT) on lung function and immune responses remains unclear. Sixty-nine older adults without participation for at least one year in structured exercise programs (aged 60-85 years) were recruited from a community extension program at a Brazilian university and randomized into an RT group (n = 31) or a control group (n = 38). This randomized controlled trial evaluated the effects of a 12-week supervised RT program performed three times per week. Primary outcomes included spirometry parameters (FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC, PEF, and FEF25-75%), respiratory muscle strength (MIP and MEP), and inflammatory biomarkers (IL-6, IL-10, TNF-α, and Klotho) in plasma and exhaled breath condensate. Secondary outcomes included handgrip strength, sit-to-stand performance, oxygen saturation, and body composition. Normally distributed outcomes were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA, whereas non-normally distributed longitudinal outcomes were analyzed using the Brunner-Langer approach for factorial longitudinal data. Between-group differences in pre-to-post changes were additionally estimated using bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. No significant Group × Time interactions were observed for spirometric parameters. Significant Group × Time interactions were observed for MIP and MEP; however, significant pre-to-post changes were observed in the control group but not in the RT group. A significant Group × Time interaction was also observed for sit-to-stand performance, with improvement in the control group but not in the RT group. No significant Group × Time interactions were observed for handgrip strength or oxygen saturation. Significant Group × Time interactions were observed for plasma IL-6, IL-10, and Klotho (all p < 0.001), as well as exhaled breath condensate IL-6 (p = 0.006) and Klotho (p = 0.003). In contrast, no significant interactions were observed for plasma TNF-α, exhaled breath condensate IL-10, or exhaled breath condensate TNF-α. Twelve weeks of supervised RT were associated with differential changes in respiratory muscle strength, functional capacity, and selected systemic and airway biomarkers in older adults. Significant Group × Time interactions were observed for MIP, MEP, the 1-min sit-to-stand test, and selected inflammatory and aging-related biomarkers, but not for pulmonary function. These findings indicate that the effects of RT varied across outcomes, rather than demonstrating consistent improvement across all assessed measures. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06682221.

title: Multi-nutrient Optimization for Skeletal Advancement and Integrated Care in Pediatric Bone Health (MOSAIC-PBH): An Expert Consensus From India.
label: approved
note: Nutrients and bone accrual in children.
abstract: Micronutrient deficiencies in children are common, often coexisting and subclinical, yet remain under-recognized. This expert consensus aims to provide an integrated framework for pediatric bone health, emphasizing multi-nutrient interactions and strategies to support adequate bone accrual and peak bone mass during growth. This consensus was developed using a modified Delphi methodology involving a multidisciplinary panel of 23 experts. A structured review of the literature was conducted to synthesize evidence on nutritional determinants, bone biology, and clinical management. Consensus statements were developed and subjected to a single-round anonymized Delphi voting process, with agreement defined as ≥75%. This expert consensus highlights the potential burden of dietary inadequacy and subclinical deficiency of key micronutrients, including vitamin D, calcium, magnesium, and zinc. Evidence supports a systems-based model of bone health, emphasizing the interdependence of structural minerals, regulatory cofactors, and hormonal pathways. A life-course approach was identified as essential, with critical windows during early life and adolescence. The panel recommends risk-based screening, comprehensive clinical assessment, and a context-specific approach to nutritional management that considers multiple nutrient and lifestyle factors for prevention and management. Practical guidance on formulation, dosing considerations, and implementation strategies is also provided. Pediatric bone health may benefit from a comprehensive, multi-nutrient and multi-mineral framework that complements assessment and management of individual nutrient deficiencies and is aligned with underlying physiology. Adoption of risk-based, life-course strategies and context-specific nutritional interventions may support skeletal health, while high-quality clinical studies are needed to establish the effects of multi-nutrient interventions on bone outcomes and fracture risk.

title: Performance and carcass traits of nursery, growing, and finishing pigs fed fourth-generation phytase superdoses in diets severely restricted in calcium and phosphorus.
label: approved
abstract: This study evaluated the effects of increasing inclusion levels of a bacterial phytase in diets with reduced calcium (Ca) and phosphorus (P) on growth performance and carcass traits of pigs across nursery, growing, and finishing phases. A total of 250 pigs (21 days of age; 6.079 ± 0.744 kg) were assigned to a randomized complete block design with five treatments: a positive control (PC), a negative control (NC; -0.18% available P and -0.16% Ca), and NC diets supplemented with 600, 1,200, or 1,800 FYT/kg. During the nursery phase, pigs fed the NC diet showed reduced average daily gain (ADG) and poorer feed conversion ratio (FCR) compared with PC (p < 0.05), whereas phytase supplementation restored performance to levels comparable to PC. Average daily feed intake was not affected (p > 0.05). In the growing and finishing phases, performance variables were affected by treatment (p < 0.05), with NC pigs showing lower ADG and worst FCR, while phytase-supplemented pigs performed similarly to PC. Across periods, quadratic responses to phytase inclusion were observed for FCR (p < 0.001), with estimated optimal levels of 1,320 and 1,404 FYT/kg during nursery and growing-finishing phases, respectively. Carcass traits were also affected by dietary treatments (p < 0.05). Pigs fed the NC diet showed lower final body weight (FBW), hot carcass weight (HCW), carcass yield (CY), and lean meat percentage (LMP) compared with PC, whereas phytase supplementation restored these variables to values comparable to PC. Quadratic responses to phytase inclusion were observed for FBW (p = 0.004), HCW (p < 0.001), CY (p = 0.028), and LMP (p < 0.001), with estimated optimal inclusion levels of 1,377, 1,324, 1,416, and 1,246 FYT/kg, respectively. In conclusion, phytase supplementation effectively mitigated the negative effects of dietary Ca and P restriction, maintaining growth performance and carcass characteristics comparable to a nutritionally adequate diet across all production phases.

title: Evaluation of factors affecting physical activity and physical function in women with primary sjogren syndrome.
label: approved
note: Physical activity and physical function in an autoimmune disease; physical function research counts.
abstract:
Objective

This study aimed to investigate the factors affecting physical activity and physical function in primary Sjogren syndrome.

Methods

In total, 63 women with primary Sjogren syndrome were examined for physical activity using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire, identified barriers to activity via the Self-Perceived Barriers for Physical Activity Questionnaire, and assessed physical function with the 30-s sit-to-stand and grip strength tests. Disease activity was measured with the EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Disease Activity Index, symptom severity with the EULAR Sjogren's Syndrome Patient Reported Index, and fatigue using the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory. Anxiety and depression levels were evaluated with the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, while health perception was assessed with the Health Perception Scale.

Results

A one-unit increase in the HPS_Center of control score was associated with a 23.1-point increase in the median International Physical Activity Questionnaire total score (95%CIs 0.55; 63.52). An increase in the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale-Anxiety, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale-Depression, and MFI_total scores is associated with a rise in the Self-Perceived Barriers for Physical Activity Questionnaire score (0.69 [0.42; 1.13]), (1.07 [0.58; 1.41]), and (0.25 [0.1; 0.3]), respectively. Conversely, grip strength was associated with EULAR Sjogren's Syndrome Patient Reported Index, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale-Depression, and MFI_Reduced Motivation (-0.44 [-0.86; -0.01]), (-0.26 [-0.41; -0.08]), and (-0.22 [-0.48; -0.08]), respectively. However, the HPS_Self-awareness score had a positive effect on the 30-s sit-to-stand (0.18 [0.11; 0.3]).

Conclusion

In women with primary Sjogren syndrome, emotional symptoms and fatigue were negatively associated with physical activity and function. Better health perception was positively associated with both. Health education and management of emotional disorders and fatigue can improve physical activity and function in primary Sjogren syndrome.

title: Effectiveness of Smartphone-Based Versus Community-Based Otago Exercise Programs for Fall Risk Reduction in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial.
label: approved
note: Otago exercise programmes for fall risk.
abstract:
Background

The Otago Exercise Program (OEP), traditionally delivered at home by a physical therapist, is an evidence-based intervention proven to reduce falls and fall-related injuries in older adults. Despite its effectiveness, widespread adoption has been limited by the personnel and resource demands required for program delivery. Exploring alternative delivery methods, including remote platforms and community-based programs, may help overcome implementation barriers and expand access to this program.

Objective

This study aims to evaluate (1) the effectiveness of 2 delivery modes of the OEP, a remotely delivered, smartphone-based program, and an in-person, community-based program, and (2) participant experiences, feasibility, and acceptability across both delivery formats.

Methods

Thirty-six adults aged 55 years or older, classified as being at intermediate or high risk for falls according to the World Falls Guidelines, will be enrolled in this study. Eligible participants will be randomly assigned to one of two intervention groups: (1) a remotely delivered, smartphone-based OEP, or (2) an in-person, community-based OEP. Participants in the community-based group will attend sessions at a senior center, whereas those in the smartphone-based group will complete the program at home via the Improve (Vipul Lugade) smartphone app. Both groups will receive individualized 60-minute training sessions twice a week for 8 weeks, delivered by certified trainers under the supervision of physical therapists. The 16-session program will include progressive balance, mobility, and strengthening exercises consistent with the OEP. The primary outcome is self-selected gait speed. Secondary outcomes include injurious falls, fall risk assessed using the Physiological Profile Assessment, Timed Up and Go, 30-Second Chair Stand, 4-Stage Balance Test, and 4-Square Step Test, as well as measures of feasibility, acceptability, usability, and health-related quality of life. Outcomes will be assessed at baseline and postintervention by investigators blinded to group allocation. In addition, gait speed will be assessed weekly throughout the 8-week intervention using the Improve app to monitor changes over time. Trainers will be blinded to outcome data, including baseline and interim assessment results.

Results

The study received funding in February 2026, and enrollment began in the same month. As of May 2026, 16 participants have been enrolled. Data collection is expected to be completed in December 2026, with findings anticipated for dissemination by the middle of 2027.

Conclusions

This is the first study to use a smartphone to deliver OEP and to directly compare remote- and community-based delivery platforms. Findings may support broader adoption and implementation of this evidence-based fall prevention program by reducing participation barriers and expanding access for older adults, particularly in remote and underserved areas.

title: Mediterranean diet and risk of prostate cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies.
label: approved
note: Mediterranean diet and prostate cancer; cancer fits no topic.
abstract:
Background

Prostate cancer is the most common malignancy among men worldwide. In addition to non-modifiable risk factors, modifiable lifestyle factors are increasingly recognized in prevention. The Mediterranean diet (Med Diet), characterized by high intake of plant-based foods, unsaturated fatty acids, and antioxidant micronutrients, has been proposed as a protective dietary pattern.

Methods

A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus examining associations between Mediterranean diet adherence and prostate cancer risk. Fourteen studies met eligibility criteria. Meta-analysis was performed in R applying a random-effects model (REML estimation; Hartung-Knapp adjustment). Heterogeneity was assessed with I² and τ²; publication bias was evaluated using a funnel plot, contour-enhanced funnel plot, and Egger's test.

Results

Based on a random effects model, we did not find a statistically significant difference in risk of prostate cancer in men with high versus low Mediterranean diet adherence (RR = 0.98; 95% CI: 0.93-1.04). Heterogeneity was moderate (Q = 19.95, I² = 34.8%). Although Egger's regression test did not indicate statistically significant publication bias (p = 0.115), complementary analyses (Q-Q plot and limit meta-analysis) suggested a possible small-study effect, warranting cautious interpretation.

Conclusion

In this meta-analysis, no protective effect of the Mediterranean diet against prostate cancer was found. Nevertheless, biological plausibility and inconsistent epidemiological trends suggest that further research using standardized dietary assessments and incorporating genetic and microbiome-related factors is needed.

Trial registration

The review protocol was not prospectively registered.

title: Sexually Dimorphic Response to Dietary Restriction-Induced Longevity and Muscle Preservation in Nothobranchius furzeri.
label: approved
note: Intermittent fasting, lifespan and muscle in killifish.
abstract: Age-related skeletal muscle decline (sarcopenia) contributes to frailty and mortality, yet how sex influences muscle aging and dietary interventions remains unclear. Using the short-lived vertebrate Nothobranchius furzeri, we investigated how sex and intermittent fasting (IF) interact to regulate lifespan and skeletal muscle aging. We establish an IF regimen that extends lifespan in both males and females, despite trade-offs including reduced growth and reproductive output. Importantly, IF improves swimming performance in aged animals of both sexes. Under normal feeding, muscle aging exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism. Males show age-associated myofiber hyperplasia, whereas females preserve fiber number but undergo hypertrophic remodeling. IF partially attenuates both phenotypes, maintaining a youthful fiber size distribution in males and females. Single-nucleus RNA-sequencing reveals sex-specific remodeling of muscle-fiber composition with age: females shift toward oxidative slow-twitch fibers under normal feeding, a change attenuated by IF, while males maintain relatively stable fiber-type proportions across diets. Cell-cell communication analyses show a global age-associated decline in intercellular signaling, with IF restoring distinct pathways in a sex-specific manner, including IGF signaling in females and metabolic ANGPTL signaling in males. Bulk transcriptomic profiling indicates largely sexually dimorphic aging trajectories, whereas IF induces both shared and sex-specific responses. Notably, IF upregulates ribosome biogenesis and genes supporting myofibrillar organization and contraction in both sexes, likely contributing to preserved muscle function. Together, these findings demonstrate that IF promotes longevity and muscle health through conserved anabolic mechanisms alongside sex-specific cellular preservation and adaptation, underscoring the importance of sex as a biological variable in interventions for healthy aging.

title: The effects of diet-induced obesity on glucose metabolism in the mouse endometrium.
label: approved
note: Diet-induced obesity and the mouse womb; fertility fits no topic.
abstract:
Background

Embryo transfer studies in women with high BMI show lower implantation rates, indicating impaired uterine function. Most mouse studies using diet-induced obesity (DIO) do not characterize the metabolomic phenotype in their models. Additionally, studies usually focus on implantation sites, ignoring the role of the epithelium in supporting embryo development. At proestrus, the uterine epithelium metabolizes glucose for its own needs and stores glycogen to support embryo development after mating. Our objectives were to (1) thoroughly characterize systemic metabolism in a long-term DIO mouse model, and (2) determine how DIO affects glucose metabolism in the uterine epithelium at proestrus.

Methods and results

Mice were randomly assigned to one of three experimental diets (10%, 45%, or 60% kcal from fat) and fed ad libitum. Both high-fat diet (HFD) groups progressively increased in body mass and glucose intolerance during the course of the experiment. After 18 weeks, the mice were sacrificed at proestrus. In serum, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) showed that HFDs altered the levels of 23 metabolites (P<0.05). Analysis of these metabolites showed enrichment in pathways related to lipids, glucose, and energy metabolism. Confirming that the HFD mice were insulin-resistant, liver glycogen stores decreased, while hepatic triglyceride levels were increased in the 60% fat group, in agreement with observations in obese people. In contrast, effects on the uterus were minimal. There was no difference in immunostaining in the uterus for the glycolytic enzymes PKM2 and PFKM. There was no difference in the glycogen levels or immunostaining for glycogen-metabolizing enzymes in the endometrium. Additionally, immunostaining for phospho-IRS and phospho-AKT in the uterine epithelium was similar across groups, indicating no change in AKT signaling in fasted mice. GC-MS analysis of the uterus found alterations in only 10 metabolites in the 60% fat group relative to the 10% fat group (P<0.05). Analysis of those metabolites found 4 pathways to be significantly enriched-glycosaminoglycan biosynthesis, mannose type O-glycan biosynthesis, linoleic acid metabolism, and purine metabolism.

Conclusion

Our DIO model resulted in systemic traits indicative of insulin resistance. However, obesity had a minimal effect on glucose metabolism in the endometrium at proestrus.

Supplementary information

The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s44494-026-00008-8.

title: Effects of resistance training on frailty-related outcomes in frail and pre-frail older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
label: approved
note: Resistance training and frailty.
abstract:
Background and objective

Frailty is associated with muscle weakness, impaired physical function, and increased risk of disability and loss of independence, making preservation of muscle function an important public health goal for healthy aging. Resistance training may help address these deficits, but its effects in frail or pre-frail older adults remain uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated its effects on muscle strength, physical function, and frailty score.

Methods

Seven electronic information sources were searched from inception to August 2026, with no language restrictions. Randomized controlled trials were included if they enrolled adults aged ≥60 years who were clearly diagnosed as frail or pre-frail using validated tools or comprehensive assessments. The intervention was limited to structured resistance training without combination with other exercise modalities. Random-effects models were used for meta-analysis, and the certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach.

Results

Nine randomized controlled trials comprising 27 study arms and 566 participants were included. Low-certainty evidence suggested that resistance training may improve knee extensor strength (SMD = 1.30, 95% CI: 0.48 to 2.13). Very-low-certainty evidence showed possible improvements in handgrip strength (MD = 4.15 kg, 95% CI: 0.81 to 7.48) and gait speed (MD = 0.13 m/s, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.26), whereas the effects on Timed Up and Go (TUG), Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) and frailty score remained uncertain. For handgrip strength, gait speed, TUG, and SPPB, clinical importance remained uncertain because the 95% CI encompassed the corresponding reference thresholds for clinical importance. Between-study heterogeneity was substantial to considerable.

Conclusion

Resistance training may improve knee extensor strength and may also benefit handgrip strength and gait speed in frail or pre-frail older adults, although the certainty of evidence is low to very low; effects on TUG, SPPB, and frailty score remain uncertain. Because muscle weakness and functional decline contribute to disability and loss of independence in later life, these findings may inform resistance-training strategies aimed at supporting muscle health and healthy aging. Further high-quality trials with standardized training prescriptions and longer-term follow-up are needed.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261391816, identifier: CRD420261391816.

title: Sulfur microbial diet and ischemic stroke risk.
label: approved
note: Dietary pattern and stroke.
abstract:
Background

This study aimed to evaluate the association of dietary pattern linked to sulfur-metabolizing gut microbiota (SMD) with incident ischemic stroke, its dose-response relationship, and population heterogeneity.

Methods

This study included 208,415 participants. The SMD score was constructed based on repeated 24-h dietary recall questionnaires (Oxford WebQ) and categorized into quartiles. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Restricted cubic spline analyses were performed to assess the dose-response relationship. Subgroup analyses, sensitivity analyses, and food substitution analyses were further conducted.

Results

During a mean follow-up of 11.45 years, a total of 3,273 incident ischemic stroke cases were identified. After full multivariable adjustment, compared with participants in the lowest quartile (Q1), those in the highest quartile (Q4) had a 13% higher hazard of ischemic stroke (HR = 1.13, 95% CI: 1.02, 1.25, p = 0.019). Each 1-standard deviation increase in the SMD score was associated with a 4% higher hazard of ischemic stroke (HR = 1.04, 95% CI: 1.01, 1.08, p = 0.018), with a significant linear trend (P for trend = 0.013). Restricted cubic spline analysis suggested an approximately linear association (P for nonlinearity = 0.232). Subgroup analyses showed heterogeneity by ethnicity (P for interaction = 0.003), whereas interactions by age and sex were not statistically significant. Sensitivity analyses yielded generally consistent estimates. Substitution analysis indicated an HR below 1 when low-calorie beverages were replaced with an equivalent energy intake of other vegetables (HR = 0.90, 95% CI: 0.81, 1.01, p = 0.063).

Conclusion

Higher adherence to the SMD was associated with a higher hazard of ischemic stroke in this large prospective cohort, with an approximately linear dose-response relationship. The association was modest and showed some sensitivity to exposure measurement precision, indicating that replication in independent cohorts is warranted.

title: Structured effects of exercise on circulating brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in postmenopausal women: a meta-analysis.
label: approved
note: Exercise and BDNF, a brain biomarker, after menopause.
abstract:
Objective

To systematically evaluate the effect of structured exercise interventions on circulating brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels among postmenopausal women, and to clarify the moderating effects of intervention modality, population characteristics, training duration, exercise intensity and energy-supply pattern on intervention outcomes, so as to provide evidence-based references for precise exercise interventions targeting brain health in postmenopausal women.

Methods

Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement, electronic databases including PubMed, Web of Science, EBSCO and CNKI were searched for original studies regarding the effects of various exercise interventions on BDNF in postmenopausal women, from database inception to August 1, 2026. The Cochrane Risk-of-Bias Tool was applied for randomized studies. For quasi-randomized and non-randomized intervention studies, we explicitly acknowledge limitations of this tool and interpret methodological assessments cautiously; studies with insufficient randomization reporting were rated as unclear risk of bias. Meta-analysis was performed using Review Manager 5.4 software. Effect sizes were presented as standardized mean difference (SMD) with 95% confidence interval (95% CI). Subgroup analysis, sensitivity analysis and publication-bias evaluation were also conducted.

Results

Twelve studies involving 351 participants were finally included, with 173 subjects in the intervention group and 178 subjects in the control group. All included trials adopted chronic long-term structured exercise interventions without acute single-bout exercise protocols. Pooled meta-analysis demonstrated that structured exercise interventions significantly elevated BDNF levels in postmenopausal women compared with control conditions [SMD = 0.64, 95% CI (0.11, 1.17), P = 0.02], with substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 81%, P < 0.0001). Subgroup analyses (only subgroups with ≥3 studies included for quantitative synthesis) indicated that intervention modality, population characteristics, training duration and energy-supply pattern were potential main sources of heterogeneity. Statistically-significant maximum effect sizes were observed in the resistance training subgroup [SMD = 1.07, 95% CI (0.12, 2.01), P = 0.03], healthy older/postmenopausal-women subgroup [SMD = 0.30, 95% CI (-0.05, 0.65), P = 0.009], anaerobic-energy-supply-predominant subgroup [SMD = 1.07, 95% CI (0.12, 2.01), P = 0.03]. Some potential moderators could not be quantitatively evaluated because corresponding subgroups contained fewer than three primary studies, and those comparisons are only discussed as exploratory clues rather than robust conclusions. Sensitivity analysis revealed no substantial shift in pooled effect direction after sequential exclusion of individual studies. Funnel-plot inspection and Egger's test detected no statistical evidence of publication asymmetry; nevertheless, these assessments were limited by the small number of included studies and cannot rule out publication bias definitively.

Conclusion

Structured exercise interventions can significantly increase peripheral BDNF levels in postmenopausal women, which suggests beneficial impacts on neuroplasticity and brain health for this population. Chronic resistance-based exercise regimens dominated by anaerobic energy-supply exert superior regulatory effects among healthy postmenopausal women.

title: Perceived Racial Discrimination Is Associated with Greater Dietary Inflammatory Potential in Children and Adolescents in the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development Study.
label: approved
note: Diet is the outcome of discrimination; no health outcome.
abstract:
Background

Perceived racial discrimination is a psychosocial stressor linked to chronic inflammation and diet-related disease risk among adults. Less is known about its effects among youth. Discrimination may influence youth chronic disease risk through dietary patterns with greater inflammatory potential, a modifiable pathway across the life course.

Objectives

This study aims to examine the association between self-reported perceived racial discrimination and dietary inflammatory potential in a large, racially and sociodemographically diverse sample of youth in the United States.

Methods

We analyzed longitudinal data from 6418 participants aged 9-12 y in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study. Perceived racial discrimination, assessed at time 1 (2018-2020) using the Youth Discrimination Measure, was modeled as a binary variable derived from a composite score, distinguishing youth reporting no discrimination from those reporting any discrimination. Children's Dietary Inflammatory Index (C-DII) scores, quantifying the inflammatory potential of dietary patterns, were derived from parent-reported 7-d food frequency questionnaires at time 1 and time 2 (2019-2021). Time 2 C-DII scores were categorized into sample-derived quartiles: Q1 reflected the lowest and Q4 reflected the highest dietary inflammatory potential. Ordinal logistic regression assessed whether time 1 discrimination predicted higher time 2 C-DII quartile, adjusting for time 1 C-DII and sociodemographic covariates.

Results

At time 1 (n = 6418), participants had a mean age of 11.97 y (SD = 0.64); 52.2% were male, and 60.5% were non-Hispanic White. Youth reporting racial discrimination at time 1 had 14% higher adjusted odds of being in a more proinflammatory C-DII quartile at time 2 than youth reporting no discrimination (odds ratio = 1.14; 95% confidence interval: 1.02, 1.26; P = 0.02).

Conclusions

Perceived racial discrimination is associated with more proinflammatory dietary patterns during early adolescence. Future studies should evaluate whether dietary patterns mediate the association between discrimination and subsequent diet-related chronic disease risks in youth.

title: Traumatic brain injury, symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction in former elite rugby players.
label: approved
abstract: While self-reported repetitive head impact (RHI) exposure in former athletes has been associated with symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction, it is uncertain whether these symptoms are mediated by changes in brain structure. We used cross-sectional data from 57 middle-aged, cognitively healthy, former elite rugby players and 114 propensity-matched controls. Questionnaires were used to collect self-reported traumatic brain injury (srTBI: blows to the head; episodes of feeling dazed and confused; episodes of loss of consciousness), RHI exposure (career length, play at the highest level and playing position), medical history, symptoms of depression (Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression scale) and sleep dysfunction (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index). Grey matter volumes and diffusion tensor imaging measures were obtained using FreeSurfer (v7.1.0, v7.4.2) and FSL (v6.0.5). We assessed how srTBI, RHI exposure, symptoms of depression, sleep dysfunction and the imaging markers were related using Spearman correlations, multivariate regression models and partial least squares structural equation modelling. Although former rugby players reported a higher number of blows to the head (9.8 versus 5.4, P < 0.001), number of episodes of feeling dazed and confused (4.5 versus 1.7, P < 0.001) and number of episodes of loss of consciousness (1.9 versus 0.7, P < 0.001), they were less likely to report a past diagnosis of anxiety (7% versus 22%, P = 0.03) or sleep disorders (2% versus 15%, P = 0.02) than controls. In rugby players, srTBI correlated poorly with RHI exposure. Furthermore, srTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with previous depression, anxiety and sleep disorders. Higher srTBI was directly associated with more symptoms of depression [B: 0.52 (95%CI: 0.21-0.74)], and indirectly associated with more sleep dysfunction [B: 0.18 (95%CI: 0.03-0.39)], fully mediated through symptoms of depression. Higher srTBI was also associated with a larger putamen (r = 0.28, P = 0.03) and inferior-tubular hypothalamus (r = 0.35, P = 0.007), thicker medial orbitofrontal (r = 0.32, P = 0.02) and insular cortices (r = 0.40, P = 0.002), lower axial diffusivity of the inferior cerebellar peduncle (r = -0.28, P = 0.03) and uncinate fasciculus (r = -0.26, P = 0.048), lower fractional anisotropy (r = -0.44, P < 0.001) and higher radial diffusivity (r = 0.29, P = 0.03) of the tapetum. Symptoms of depression were associated with thicker superior (r = 0.30, P = 0.02) and inferior (r = 0.33, P = 0.01) parietal cortices, higher fractional anisotropy of the hippocampal cingulum (r = 0.27, P = 0.04) and lower mean diffusivity of the fornix (r = -0.28, P = 0.03). None of these imaging markers mediated the association between srTBI and symptoms of depression. SrTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with symptoms of depression in former rugby players. However, this relationship was not mediated through differences in brain structure, suggesting that psychosocial or methodological factors such as recall bias and common method bias may be more important.

title: Dietary aromatic amino acids, their food sources, and incident hypertension in Chinese adults: a prospective cohort study.
label: approved
note: Dietary amino acids and hypertension.
abstract:
Background

Prospective evidence linking dietary aromatic amino acids (AAAs), including phenylalanine (Phe), tyrosine (Tyr), and tryptophan (Trp), to incident hypertension currently remains limited, particularly regarding their individual components and food sources. Herein, we examined the association between dietary AAAs, their food sources, and incident hypertension among Chinese adults.

Methods

Using the China Health and Nutrition Survey database, this prospective cohort study collected data from 10,087 adults without hypertension at baseline. Baseline dietary intake was assessed using three consecutive 24-h dietary recalls, combined with household food weighing; the energy-adjusted AAA intake was expressed in g/1,000 kcal. Incident hypertension was defined as measured blood pressure, physician diagnosis, or use of antihypertensive medication. Mixed-effects Cox proportional hazards models with household identifiers as random intercepts were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Dose-response, food-source-specific, subgroup, and sensitivity analyses were performed.

Results

During the 95,153 person-years of follow-up, 3,531 participants developed hypertension. In fully adjusted models, the highest quartile of total AAA intake was associated with a modestly higher risk of incident hypertension compared with the lowest quartile (HR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.03-1.31; P for trend = 0.006). Positive associations were more consistent for Phe (HR for Q4 vs. Q1, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.11-1.44) and Trp (HR, 1.29; 95% CI, 1.14-1.46) individually, while Tyr intake showed no significant association with hypertension. Dose-response analyses indicated approximately linear positive associations for total AAA, Phe, and Trp. The association for total AAA was attenuated following additional adjustment for baseline province (HR for Q4 vs. Q1, 1.10; 95% CI, 0.97-1.24), while the positive associations for Phe and Trp persisted. Cereals were the predominant contributors to AAA intake, and plant-derived Phe and Trp were positively associated with the risk of hypertension.

Conclusion

Higher dietary intakes of Phe and Trp showed consistent positive associations with incident hypertension, while Tyr showed no clear association. The modest association for total AAA was attenuated after adjusting for baseline province and should therefore be interpreted cautiously in relation to potential regional confounding factors. These findings support the component-specific interpretation of dietary AAAs and consideration of their regional and food source contexts.

title: Mediterranean-ketogenic vs. medium-chain triglyceride supplemented Mediterranean diet: Effects on the gut-brain-immune axis in Parkinson's disease.
label: approved
note: Mediterranean-ketogenic diet in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Ketogenic diets have been proposed as potential neuroprotective interventions for Parkinson's disease (PD), but concerns remain regarding their effects on the gut microbiome and gut-brain-immune axis. We conducted a randomized crossover trial comparing 8-week Mediterranean-ketogenic (MeDi-KD) versus medium-chain triglyceride-supplemented Mediterranean (MeDi-MCT) diets, separated by an 8-week washout (NCT05469997). Primary outcomes included changes in gut microbiome taxonomic and functional profiles, fecal short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, and biomarkers of intestinal permeability and inflammation. Neither intervention significantly altered microbiome diversity or functional gene abundance, established features of PD-associated dysbiosis, nor fecal or plasma biomarkers of intestinal permeability (zonulin) or inflammation (calprotectin). The MeDi-KD modestly reduced total fecal SCFAs, while both interventions increased the relative abundance of Roseburia hominis, and the MeDi-MCT was associated with decreases in plasma IL-1β and IL-8. No severe adverse events were reported, supporting further investigation of MeDi-KD strategies in larger, longer-duration PD trials.

title: Functions of vitamin B3 and its metabolites in epigenetic regulation.
label: approved
note: Vitamin B3 and epigenetic gene regulation, mechanisms only.
abstract: Recent research advances point toward an intimate connection between metabolic chemistry and molecular mechanisms of epigenetic gene regulation that modulates cellular functions. Many small molecule metabolites generated through metabolic pathways are demonstrated to have the ability or potential to bind or modify nuclear chromatin, chromatin-modifying enzymes, or other chromatin associated proteins. These processes cause alterations of chromatin dynamics, gene expression, and other DNA-templated functions, which ultimately lead to phenotypic changes of the cell. Vitamin B3 is an essential micronutrient of the human diet required for normal physiological function, but the dysregulation of vitamin B3 metabolism has been found in association with several pathological conditions. Intracellularly, vitamin B3 is metabolized into various intermediate metabolites, several of which are functional molecules that have been found to exert an influence on epigenetic regulation of gene function. Multiple lines of experimental evidence show that vitamin B3, and these functional metabolites, can directly or indirectly influence histone post-translational modification, DNA methylation, and alter chromatin remodeling and gene expression. The appreciation of vitamin B3's roles in epigenetic regulation provides a novel framework for understanding diet- and metabolism-driven mechanisms of gene program control. In this review, we discuss the current understanding of vitamin B3 metabolic pathways, biochemical characteristics of various B3-derived intermediates, and their distinctive mechanisms in epigenetic regulation concluding with a reflection on problems, challenges, and prospects in this field.

title: Effects of vitamin D supplementation on vitamin D status and physical performance in football players: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
label: approved
note: Vitamin D and performance in football players.
abstract:
Background/objectives

Low vitamin D status is frequently reported among athletes, but whether vitamin D supplementation improves physical performance in football players remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of vitamin D supplementation on serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] concentration, jump performance, sprint performance, aerobic capacity, and muscular performance in association football and futsal players.

Methods

PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from database inception to 31 May 2026. Controlled intervention studies comparing vitamin D supplementation with control conditions were eligible. Standardized mean differences were calculated as Hedges' g and pooled using random-effects meta-analyses. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias using RoB 2 or ROBINS-I. The certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261430873).

Results

Eleven reports representing nine independent studies and 312 players were included. In RCT-only primary analyses, vitamin D supplementation was associated with higher circulating 25(OH)D concentrations (g = 1.41, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.92; I² = 58.0%). Pooled effects were not statistically significant for jump performance (g = 0.21, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.53), sprint performance (g = -0.03, 95% CI -0.40 to 0.34), aerobic capacity (g = 0.00, 95% CI -0.45 to 0.45), or muscular performance (g = 0.19, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.51). The certainty of evidence was low for circulating 25(OH)D, jump performance, and muscular performance, and very low for sprint performance and aerobic capacity.

Conclusions

Vitamin D supplementation was associated with increased circulating 25(OH)D concentrations, whereas current evidence is insufficient to support a consistent improvement in physical performance. Given the low to very low certainty of evidence, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Larger, well-designed randomized controlled trials using standardized, football-relevant performance tests are warranted.

title: BSJPHXF modulates the FGF23-Klotho bone-kidney axis and calcium-phosphorus metabolism in ovariectomized rats with postmenopausal osteoporosis.
label: approved
note: Herbal medicine formula, closer to a drug than diet.
abstract:
Objective

To investigate the effects of the Kidney-Tonifying, Spleen-Strengthening and Blood-Activating Formula (BSJPHXF, also known as Gukang Formula) on the FGF23-Klotho bone-kidney axis and calcium-phosphorus metabolism in a rat model of postmenopausal osteoporosis.

Methods

Forty SPF female Sprague-Dawley rats were randomly divided into sham-operated, ovariectomized (OVX; model), BSJPHXF and Liuwei Dihuang Wan (LWDHW; positive control) groups (n=10 per group) and treated by gavage for 4 weeks after a 12-week recovery period. Serum calcium and phosphorus were measured by automated biochemical analysis; serum FGF23, parathyroid hormone (PTH) and 1, 25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 [1, 25-(OH)2D3] by ELISA; renal Klotho, NaPi-IIa and 1α-hydroxylase (Cyp27b1) by Western blot; bone microstructure by Micro-CT; and renal histopathology by HE staining. Serum biochemistry and ELISA were performed in nine animals per group, and Western blot, Micro-CT and histology in three animals per group; the animal was the experimental unit.

Results

Compared with sham, OVX rats had lower serum calcium (1.997 ± 0.109 vs. 2.547 ± 0.189 mmol/L) and 1, 25-(OH)2D3 (102.21 ± 2.87 vs. 201.74 ± 5.85 pg/mL) and higher serum phosphorus (2.019 ± 0.099 vs. 1.355 ± 0.027 mmol/L), FGF23 (366.82 ± 28.36 vs. 159.52 ± 20.39 pg/mL) and PTH (141.63 ± 15.29 vs. 33.91 ± 7.59 pg/mL) (all P<0.001). BSJPHXF attenuated these changes relative to OVX (P<0.001). BSJPHXF and LWDHW did not differ for calcium, FGF23 or PTH, whereas LWDHW produced a greater reduction in serum phosphorus (1.463 ± 0.062 vs. 1.587 ± 0.048 mmol/L, P = 0.0015) and a greater increase in 1, 25-(OH)2D3 (174.66 ± 7.00 vs. 156.54 ± 13.09 pg/mL, P = 0.0002). On Micro-CT, BSJPHXF, but not LWDHW, improved trabecular bone volume fraction, separation and number versus OVX, and BSJPHXF was superior to LWDHW for all three; trabecular thickness did not differ among groups.

Conclusion

In OVX rats, BSJPHXF attenuated calcium-phosphorus disturbance, with accompanying changes in renal Klotho, NaPi-IIa and Cyp27b1 and in circulating FGF23, PTH and 1, 25-(OH)2D3, and improved trabecular microarchitecture. As the mechanistically most important endpoints rested on three animals per group and functional renal parameters were not measured, these findings are preliminary and hypothesis-generating.

title: Uncontrolled metabolic syndrome associated with poorer sleep quality in adults in rural areas: a secondary analysis.
label: approved
note: Metabolic syndrome and sleep, no diet or exercise exposure.
abstract:
Objective

To examine whether clinical management of metabolic syndrome (MetS) is associated with sleep health among adults receiving care in rural primary care settings.

Methods

This cross-sectional analysis used baseline data from adults (age 20-75 years; body mass index (BMI) 30-45 kg/m2) enrolled in the RE-POWER trial, a pragmatic behavioral weight loss intervention implemented in rural primary care clinics. Sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). MetS was defined according to American Heart Association/National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (AHA/NHLBI) criteria and categorized as: (1) no-MetS, (2) controlled MetS (criteria met via medication use), and (3) uncontrolled MetS (criteria met via abnormal laboratory values). Linear mixed models evaluated whether MetS status predicted global PSQI, PSQI subcomponents, and sleep duration, adjusting for age, sex, and BMI.

Results

Among 1406 adults (mean age 54.6 ± 11.8 years; 76.8% female), those with uncontrolled MetS (n = 634) had significantly worse global PSQI, sleep latency, and sleep disturbance scores compared with adults without MetS (n = 483) (P < .05). Sleep outcomes did not differ between adults with controlled MetS (n = 289) and those without MetS (P > .05).

Conclusion

Poorly controlled MetS was associated with poorer sleep quality, whereas clinically controlled MetS was not. Future research is needed to determine if effective clinical management of MetS may confer benefits for sleep health in rural populations.

title: Effects of a 4-week vinyasa yoga intervention on sleep and cardiovascular health in adults with insomnia symptoms: a pilot randomized controlled trial.
label: approved
note: Yoga, sleep and cardiovascular health.
abstract:
Study objectives

Vinyasa yoga (VY) yields moderate-intensity physical activity that may improve sleep and cardiovascular health (CVH). However, evidence is scarce regarding the effects of VY on CVH. This study examined the effects of a 4-week VY intervention on sleep and CVH in adults with insomnia symptoms.

Materials and methods

A total of 33 insufficiently active adults (84.8 per cent female; 78.8 per cent White; 34.9 ± 10.6 y; 28.9 kg/m2) with insomnia symptoms (Insomnia Severity Index [ISI] ≥10) were randomized to a 4-week VY intervention (n = 17) or non-active control (CON; n = 16). VY participants practiced 3×/week following pre-recorded 60-minute videos and CON maintained their current lifestyle. Resting daytime blood pressure (BP), heart rate (HR), and HR variability (HRV) were obtained at baseline and post-intervention. Sleep was measured using the ISI, actigraphy, and a sleep diary. One night during sleep assessment, participants wore a chest HR monitor to assess HRV; primary HRV outcome was root mean square of successive differences. Analyses used linear mixed models and Cohen's d effect sizes.

Results

Changes in ISI, actigraphy-, and diary-assessed sleep from baseline to post-intervention did not differ between groups (each p > .06). Changes in nocturnal HRV and daytime resting BP and HRV were not significant (each p ≥ .30). Resting HR decreased for VY (72.41 ± 2.92 to 69.50 ± 2.60 bpm) and increased for CON (70.47 ± 2.54 to 72.93 ± 2.60 bpm) (p = .047). Additionally, among highly adherent participants, VY reduced ISI scores more than CON (p = .002).

Conclusion

VY improves insomnia symptoms among those who practice regularly. It does not appear to improve nocturnal cardiovascular physiology, and shows modest benefits on daytime cardiac parasympathetic activity.

Clinical trial registration

Registry: ClinicalTrials.gov; Name: Yoga for Insomnia Study; URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05723211; Registration ID: NCT0572321; Date of Registration: January 2, 2023.
